problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs above, where $t\in R.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ The function $a(t)=[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1-t\end{aligned}]$ 
{{field-1}} 
a solution of the system.

$\,$ The function $b(t)=[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+1 \\ -t\end{aligned}]$ 
{{field-2}} 
a solution of the system.

$\,$ The function $c(t)=[\begin{aligned}t+1 \\ -t\end{aligned}]$ 
{{field-3}} 
a solution of the system.

$\,$ {{field-4}} 
is a set of fundamental solutions to the system because the Wronskian 

$$
W({{field-5}})={{field-6}}\ne 0
$$

$\,$ for at least one $t\in R.$
worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})$ of two vector-valued functions 

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- $a(t)=[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1-t\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(t)^{′} \\ (1-t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t \\ 1-t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1\cdot t+1\cdot (1-t) \\ -1\cdot t+(-1)\cdot (1-t)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+1 \\ -t\end{aligned}]$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({t}^{2}+1)^{′} \\ (-t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+1 \\ -t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2t \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)+1\cdot (-t) \\ -1\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)+(-1)\cdot (-t)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2t \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-t+1 \\ -{t}^{2}+t-1\end{aligned}]\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=[\begin{aligned}t+1 \\ -t\end{aligned}]$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(t+1)^{′} \\ (-t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t+1 \\ -t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1\cdot (t+1)+1\cdot (-t) \\ -1\cdot (t+1)+(-1)\cdot (-t)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,b}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,c) & =|\begin{aligned}t & t+1 \\ 1-t & -t\end{aligned}| \\  & =t\cdot (-t)-(t+1)\cdot (1-t) \\  & =-{t}^{2}-1+{t}^{2} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one $t\in R,$ ${a,c}$ is a set of fundamental solutions of the system.
